title: IIT Bombay Students Begin Hunger Strike, Demand Accountability in Sahil Wakode's Death
excerpt: Weeks after second-year student Sahil Wakode was found dead in his hostel room, students at IIT Bombay have begun a hunger strike demanding a credible investigation into allegations of caste-based harassment and a biased internal probe.
body:
• Students at IIT Bombay have begun a hunger strike after weeks of protests over the death of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode, found dead in his hostel room on September 18, hours after he was caught with a mobile phone during a mid-semester exam.
  • Wakode's parents allege he faced caste-based harassment for months. A police FIR names exam invigilator Professor Suryanarayana Doolla for abetment to suicide, with SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act provisions invoked.
  • The Mumbai Crime Branch has taken over the investigation, while students demand the institute's 10-member internal inquiry panel be reconstituted, alleging some members publicly backed Doolla before the probe concluded.
  • IIT Bombay has sent Doolla on leave, apologised for earlier statements linking the death to the exam incident, and postponed mid-semester examinations to October 10-11.

Students at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay have begun a hunger strike demanding accountability from the administration over the death of Sahil Wakode, a second-year BTech student whose death on September 18 has triggered weeks of campus protests and a criminal investigation.

Wakode, 20, a student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering, was found dead in his hostel room on the evening of September 18, hours after he was caught with a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination. The institute initially stated that he had used the phone to access ChatGPT for answers. No suicide note was recovered.

"Those who tortured my son should be put behind bars. He had told us that he repeatedly faced caste discrimination at the institute."

— Ravindra Wakode, Sahil Wakode's father

Context & Background

The case took shape in the days after September 18, when Wakode's parents alleged that their son had faced caste-based harassment and sustained mental pressure for months before his death. Based on their complaint, police registered a case of abetment to suicide against Professor Suryanarayana Doolla, who was invigilating the examination, and invoked the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The parents also sought action against the institute's director.

Wakode's parents, Ravindra and Sonali Wakode, began their own indefinite hunger strike at Mumbai's Azad Maidan on September 24. Police had detained Ravindra Wakode while he was travelling toward the IIT Bombay campus to begin the protest; the parents were later taken for a meeting with Kishor Makwana, chairperson of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, which has taken suo motu cognizance of the matter. They ended the strike later that night but said they would resume it if their demands were not met.

"I do not care, even if I get arrested. My son should get justice constitutionally. This is the state of Chhatrapati Shivaji, Phule, Shahu and Ambedkar."

— Ravindra Wakode, announcing a sit-in protest at Azad Maidan

The institute's early communications drew sharp criticism. IIT Bombay subsequently apologised for public statements that linked the death closely to the examination incident, noting that the full circumstances remained under investigation. The board constituted a 10-member committee, but students and the family have questioned its composition, alleging some members publicly backed Professor Doolla before the probe concluded. The panel has been granted a one-week extension, according to reports.

Impact & Analysis

The protests have already forced administrative responses. Professor Doolla has been sent on leave — and his deanship suspended — to allow an impartial probe. The institute postponed mid-semester examinations from September 26-27 to October 10-11, buying time for a committee with student representation to draft clearer misconduct-handling guidelines.

Student groups including the Ambedkar Periyar Phule Study Circle have demanded the committee be dissolved and reconstituted with external members and greater SC/ST representation. A candlelight march on campus drew students from multiple premier institutes, whose unions have backed the Wakode family. Investigators have recorded statements from students and staff, collected CCTV footage, and sent Wakode's locked iPhone to the Kalina Forensic Science Laboratory for technical analysis, according to reports.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian families abroad, the case lands close to home: IITs remain the aspiration behind countless NRI households' education plans, and diaspora parents follow closely how elite Indian campuses handle student welfare and accountability. The demands on the table — transparent probes, external oversight, clearer misconduct procedures — mirror reforms diaspora alumni have pushed for at Western universities after campus deaths.

What's Next

Three parallel processes will determine what follows: the Crime Branch investigation, including forensic analysis of the phone and CCTV footage; the National Commission for Scheduled Castes' inquiry, after chairman Kishor Makwana's spot visit to the campus on September 24; and the institute's internal panel, whose credibility depends on whether the administration reconstitutes it with external membership. Wakode's parents have said they will resume their protest if action stalls, and the rescheduled October 10-11 examinations give the institute a short window to publish the clearer misconduct-handling guidelines it has promised.
image_caption: Sahil Wakode's parents sit on a hunger strike holding his portrait, beneath a banner reading "Hunger Strike Day-4, Justice for Sahil". They allege he faced caste-based harassment at IIT Bombay and are demanding action against those named in the police complaint.
nri_angle: NRI families track IIT campus accountability closely; the case tests whether elite Indian institutions offer transparent probes and external oversight that diaspora parents expect.
